plain_text: Before DNA and proteins, short RNA strands may have copied themselves. In the lab, an RNA enzyme about 200 letters long can copy RNA strands nearly its own length.
mechanism: Template-directed copying by an RNA enzyme
source: Wochner et al. (2011) Science 332:209; Eigen (1971) Naturwissenschaften 58:465
note: No fossil can record this. A copier must make fewer than about one error per genome, or its information melts away (Eigen's error threshold).

plain_text: Every living cell reads DNA in three-letter words: 64 words for 20 building blocks of protein. A code shared by all life must be older than their last common ancestor.
mechanism: Triplet codons read by transfer RNA on the ribosome
source: Crick (1968) J. Mol. Biol. 38:367; Koonin & Novozhilov (2009) IUBMB Life 61:99
note: Dated by inference to before the last universal common ancestor.

plain_text: The last ancestor shared by all living things already stored about 2.5 million DNA letters and some 2,600 protein genes, about the size of a modern bacterium.
mechanism: Double-stranded DNA genome copied by proteins
source: Moody et al. (2024) Nat. Ecol. Evol. 8:1654
note: Genome size 2.49-2.99 million letters. The date is a molecular clock calibrated on fossils.

plain_text: Bacteria and archaea pass genes sideways, not only to offspring. About four in five genes in a microbial genome have been swapped at some point in their history.
mechanism: Uptake of loose DNA, transfer by viruses and cell-to-cell mating
source: Dagan, Artzy-Randrup & Martin (2008) PNAS 105:10039; Blattner et al. (1997) Science 277:1453
note: About 18% of E. coli's genes arrived after it split from Salmonella (Lawrence & Ochman 1998 PNAS 95:9413).

plain_text: Archaea that turn carbon dioxide and hydrogen into methane leave a chemical signature in rocks 3.46 billion years old. Their living relatives carry compact genomes of under 2 million letters.
mechanism: Compact genome; archaeal DNA copying machinery
source: Ueno et al. (2006) Nature 440:516; Bult et al. (1996) Science 273:1058
note: The rock signature is chemical, not a fossil cell.

plain_text: Cyanobacteria gained the genes to split water with sunlight and release oxygen. Oxygen built up in the air by 2.43 billion years ago, so the genes are at least that old.
source: Kaneko et al. (1996) DNA Res. 3:109; Fournier et al. (2021) Proc. R. Soc. B 288:20210675
note: The Great Oxidation sets the youngest possible date; clocks put the origin earlier.

milestone: Mitochondria hand genes to the nucleus
plain_title: A captured bacterium gives up its genes
plain_text: The bacterium that became the mitochondrion once had thousands of genes. Most moved to the host's nucleus or were lost: the most bacteria-like mitochondrion keeps 97 genes, ours keeps 37.
mechanism: Gene transfer from organelle to nucleus
source: Lang et al. (1997) Nature 387:493; Anderson et al. (1981) Nature 290:457; Timmis et al. (2004) Nat. Rev. Genet. 5:123
note: Human mitochondrial DNA: 16,569 letters, 13 protein genes. Earliest firm complex-cell fossils are about 1.65 billion years old.

milestone: The complex cell and its packed chromosomes
plain_text: Complex cells wrap DNA around protein spools and keep it in a nucleus, which lets genomes grow far larger. The common ancestor of complex cells already had several thousand gene families.
source: Goffeau et al. (1996) Science 274:546; Koonin (2010) Genome Biol. 11:209; Miao et al. (2019) Precambrian Res. 321:172
note: The date is the oldest firm fossil of a complex cell; molecular clocks put the ancestor earlier.

milestone: Chloroplast genes move into plant nuclei
plain_text: Plants and algae captured a cyanobacterium that became the chloroplast. About 18% of the genes in a plant's nucleus came from it.
mechanism: Gene transfer from organelle to nucleus
source: Martin et al. (2002) PNAS 99:12246; Sato et al. (1999) DNA Res. 6:283; Bengtson et al. (2017) PLoS Biol. 15:e2000735
note: 1.6 billion-year-old fossils may be red algae (debated); Bangiomorpha at 1.05 billion years is certain.

plain_text: Sex mixes two parents' genomes and shuffles them in every generation, so good combinations form and bad mutations can be purged. The oldest fossil with sexual reproduction is a red alga.
source: Gibson et al. (2018) Geology 46:135; Butterfield (2000) Paleobiology 26:386; Ramesh, Malik & Logsdon (2005) Curr. Biol. 15:185
note: Meiosis genes trace to the common ancestor of complex cells, so sex is probably older.

plain_text: Green algae, the group land plants grew from, were already living as small seaweeds a billion years ago. A living single-celled green alga carries about 18,000 genes.
mechanism: Chloroplast genes plus a large nuclear genome
source: Tang et al. (2020) Nat. Ecol. Evol. 4:543; Merchant et al. (2007) Science 318:245
note: Date is Proterocladus, the oldest green seaweed fossil.

plain_text: Fungi grow as threads that can stretch for kilometres. A fungus that lives on bread mould today carries about 10,000 genes; the oldest fungus-like fossils are nearly a billion years old.
source: Loron et al. (2019) Nature 570:232; Galagan et al. (2003) Nature 422:859
note: The fossil's fungal nature rests on chitin in its walls.

plain_text: Choanoflagellates, the closest single-celled relatives of animals, already carry genes for sticking cells together and passing signals, long before the first animal body.
source: King et al. (2008) Nature 451:783; dos Reis et al. (2015) Curr. Biol. 25:2939
note: Date is the clock estimate for the animal-choanoflagellate ancestor.

plain_title: Sponges: a big genome for a simple body
plain_text: A sponge has no nerves or muscles, yet its genome holds about 30,000 genes, including many that animals later used for nerves and immunity.
source: Srivastava et al. (2010) Nature 466:720; Love et al. (2009) Nature 457:718
note: The 635 million-year-old sponge chemical marker is debated.

plain_text: A sea anemone, a jellyfish relative, has about 18,000 genes and shares much of its gene order with humans: the animal toolkit was largely set early.
mechanism: Conserved gene families and gene order
source: Putnam et al. (2007) Science 317:86; Liu et al. (2014) Proc. R. Soc. B 281:20141202
note: Date is the oldest likely cnidarian fossil, Haootia.

plain_title: Genes that lay out a body
plain_text: Animals with a head and a tail use a row of Hox genes to mark where each body part goes. The earliest such animals left trails and fossils 555 million years ago.
source: Lewis (1978) Nature 276:565; Evans et al. (2020) PNAS 117:7845; Adams et al. (2000) Science 287:2185
note: Date is Ikaria, the oldest bilaterian fossil.

plain_text: The roundworm C. elegans has about 1,000 cells and about 20,000 genes, almost as many as we have. Gene number does not grow with body complexity.
source: C. elegans Sequencing Consortium (1998) Science 282:2012
note: Roundworm fossils are rare; the row sits beside the 530 Ma steering milestone it illustrates.

milestone: Two genome doublings in early vertebrates
plain_text: Early vertebrates copied their entire genome twice. The spare copies of genes were free to take on new jobs, many of them in the brain and senses.
source: Dehal & Boore (2005) PLoS Biol. 3:e314; Putnam et al. (2008) Nature 453:1064; Simakov et al. (2020) Nat. Ecol. Evol. 4:820
note: The lancelet shows the genome before the doublings; we carry up to four copies of many of its genes.

plain_text: Spores show plants on land by 470 million years ago. A living moss, close to those first land plants, carries about 33,000 genes, more than we do, including new ones for drought and ultraviolet light.
mechanism: Gene families for life out of water
source: Wellman, Osterloff & Mohiuddin (2003) Nature 425:282; Lang et al. (2018) Plant J. 93:515
note: The tree places land plants at 400 Ma, where large vascular plants spread; the first spores are older.

plain_text: The Australian lungfish carries about 43 billion DNA letters, 14 times ours, swollen by copies of jumping genes. Its lineage goes back 400 million years.
source: Meyer et al. (2021) Nature 590:284
note: The genome is measured in the living fish; when it grew is unknown.

milestone: A third doubling in bony fish
plain_text: The ancestor of most living fish doubled its genome once more. Zebrafish still carry two copies of many genes we have only once.
source: Jaillon et al. (2004) Nature 431:946; Howe et al. (2013) Nature 496:498

plain_text: Seed plants doubled their whole genome about 319 million years ago and flowering plants again about 192 million years ago. Plants double far more often than animals.
source: Jiao et al. (2011) Nature 473:97; Arabidopsis Genome Initiative (2000) Nature 408:796

milestone: Small genomes in dinosaurs and birds
plain_text: The size of bone cells in fossils tracks genome size. It shows that small genomes, typical of birds today, arose in two-legged dinosaurs long before flight.
source: Organ et al. (2007) Nature 446:180; International Chicken Genome Sequencing Consortium (2004) Nature 432:695

plain_text: Flowering plants appear as fossil pollen about 130 million years ago and soon dominate the land. Amborella, the living plant closest to their root, carries about 27,000 genes.
mechanism: Repeated genome doublings and gene families for flowers
source: Amborella Genome Project (2013) Science 342:1241089; Hughes (1994) The Enigma of Angiosperm Origins

plain_text: About 3.1 billion DNA letters and some 20,000 protein genes. Nearly half of it is copies of old jumping genes. Each child carries about 70 new letter changes.
mechanism: Diploid genome with large repeated regions
source: Nurk et al. (2022) Science 376:44; Lander et al. (2001) Nature 409:860; Hublin et al. (2017) Nature 546:289
note: Date is the oldest Homo sapiens fossil (Jebel Irhoud).

plain_text: Bread wheat carries three grass genomes in one, about 17 billion letters, from crosses between wild grasses in farmers' fields about 10,000 to 8,000 years ago.
source: International Wheat Genome Sequencing Consortium (2018) Science 361:eaar7191
note: The dates are archaeological.

plain_text: In 1977 the first complete genome, a virus of 5,386 letters, was read letter by letter.
source: Sanger et al. (1977) Nature 265:687

milestone: The first genome of a living cell
plain_text: In 1995 the full genome of a bacterium, 1.8 million letters, was read for the first time.
source: Fleischmann et al. (1995) Science 269:496

plain_text: The Human Genome Project finished in 2003; the last gaps were closed in 2022.
source: International Human Genome Sequencing Consortium (2004) Nature 431:931; Nurk et al. (2022) Science 376:44

plain_text: In 2010 a bacterial genome of about 1.08 million letters was written chemically and booted up in a cell.
source: Gibson et al. (2010) Science 329:52
note: In 2016 a pared-down version ran on 473 genes (Hutchison et al. 2016 Science 351:aad6253).

plain_text: In 2012 a bacterial defence system, CRISPR, was turned into a tool that cuts DNA at a chosen spot.
source: Jinek et al. (2012) Science 337:816

plain_text: A book was written into DNA in 2012; by 2017 the method reached about 215 million gigabytes per gram.
source: Church, Gao & Kosuri (2012) Science 337:1628; Erlich & Zielinski (2017) Science 355:950

plain_text: The pond protist Paramecium makes about one copying error per 50 billion DNA letters per generation, the lowest rate measured. Large populations let selection push accuracy that far.
mechanism: Proofreading and repair under strong selection
source: Sung et al. (2012) PNAS 109:19339; Aury et al. (2006) Nature 444:171
note: Measured today. Larger populations push mutation rates lower (the drift-barrier idea, Lynch 2010 Trends Genet. 26:345).

plain_text: A small fern from New Caledonia holds about 160 billion DNA letters, 50 times ours. Genome size and complexity part ways.
source: Fernández et al. (2024) iScience 27:109889; Pellicer et al. (2010) Bot. J. Linn. Soc. 164:10
note: The previous record was the plant Paris japonica, about 149 billion letters.

plain_text: Bacteria that live inside insect cells have lost almost every gene they could borrow from their host. One keeps only about 137 protein genes.
source: Bennett & Moran (2013) Genome Biol. Evol. 5:1675
note: Free-living bacteria need at least about 1.3 million letters.

plain_text: Soil myxobacteria hunt in packs and build fruiting bodies. One carries 14.8 million letters, more than baker's yeast.
mechanism: Large genome with many regulatory genes
source: Han et al. (2013) Sci. Rep. 3:2101
